content: The facility, originally established by the United States Army during World War I, was located in Aurora, Colorado, covering an area of 3 square kilometers. It was founded to address the urgent need for treating the large number of casualties resulting from chemical weapons used in Europe during the war. Denver's reputation as a leading center for tuberculosis treatment motivated local citizens to advocate for the Army to select Denver as the site for the new hospital. Initially named Army Hospital 21, it was formally dedicated in the autumn of 1918 in Aurora, which at the time had a population of fewer than 1,000 residents. In July 1920, the facility was renamed Fitzsimons Army Hospital in honor of Lieutenant William T. Fitzsimons, the first American officer killed in World War I. During World War II, the hospital played a critical role in treating returning casualties and became one of the Army's premier medical training centers. In the 1950s, President Dwight D. Eisenhower received treatment at the facility on three separate occasions for his heart condition. Notably, in September 1955, while vacationing in Denver, he suffered a myocardial infarction and was treated in an oxygen tent at the hospital. In 2000, a suite of rooms on the hospital's eighth floor was restored to replicate its appearance during Eisenhower's recovery. The facility also holds historical significance as the birthplace of U.S. Senator and 2004 presidential candidate John Kerry, who was born there on December 11, 1943, while his father was receiving treatment for tuberculosis. In July 1995, the Base Realignment and Closure Commission recommended the closure of the facility, with the exception of the Edgar J. McWhethy Army Reserve Center located at the southeast corner of the installation. The closure was completed in 1999. The site underwent a $744-million redevelopment for civilian use, which included the construction of the University of Colorado Hospital's $110-million Anschutz Outpatient Pavilion and the $509-million Children's Hospital. Additional facilities built on the site included the Veterans Administration Medical Center. Portions of the property were transferred to the city of Aurora, Colorado, allowing the city to repurpose buildings and land for its new police academy. The facility was also home to the United States Army Medical Equipment and Optical School (USAMEOS). This institution trained technicians in Biomedical Equipment Repair and Optical Laboratory Operations. Biomedical Equipment Repair personnel, known as BMETs (pronounced bee-mets), were assigned to military medical units to install, maintain, repair, and calibrate advanced life support, diagnostic, imaging, and general medical equipment. Military Occupational Specialties (MOS) graduating from USAMEOS included 35G, 35S, 35T, and later 35U. The training program at USAMEOS was divided into Basic and Advanced Courses. The Basic Course lasted 20 weeks, while the Advanced Course extended to 32 weeks. With additional coursework, graduates could earn an Associate of Applied Science (AAS) degree in Biomedical Equipment Maintenance from Regis College in Denver. After completing the Basic Course, students were typically assigned to operational units for practical experience before returning for the Advanced Course. Graduates of USAMEOS were highly sought after as skilled technicians in the industry. The technical training provided at USAMEOS was rigorous, combining engineering theory with hands-on learning in extensive laboratory settings. The hallways of the training facility displayed photographs of graduating BMET classes, commemorating decades of operation.
